Introduction

Have you ever walked into a school toilet and the lights came on automatically? Or noticed that lamps along the road only switch on when it gets dark? Those are examples of 'smart' lighting - lights with sensors that switch themselves on and off. In this worksheet you will learn the basics.
Theory

A SMART light is a light that has a small electronic brain and at least one sensor. The brain decides when to switch the light on or off based on what the sensor measures. So you don't need to flip a switch any more.
The two most common sensors used in lighting are:

A MOTION SENSOR detects movement. As soon as somebody walks in, it tells the light to turn on. After a few minutes of no movement, it tells the light to turn off again. (The few-minute delay is so the light does not switch off if you sit still for a moment.)
A DAYLIGHT SENSOR measures how much daylight is in the room. When the sun goes down or it gets cloudy, it tells the light to turn on. When daylight is enough, it tells the light to turn off.

Both sensors save energy in DIFFERENT WAYS. A motion sensor saves energy in rooms that are sometimes used and sometimes empty (toilets, corridors, storerooms). A daylight sensor saves energy in rooms with windows where the lights are sometimes on while the sun is shining (offices, classrooms with big windows, shop displays).
Sometimes you use BOTH sensors together. For example: a hallway with a window. The light should only turn on if (1) somebody is walking in AND (2) it is dark enough that they need the light.
Worked example
*A storage room is currently lit for 8 hours per day, even though it is only entered briefly twice a day for ~5 minutes each.*
**Step 1:** Without sensor: lights on 8 hours per day.
**Step 2:** With motion sensor: lights on roughly 2 × 5 min = 10 min per day = ~0.17 hours per day.
**Step 3:** Energy reduction: from 8 h to 0.17 h is about 98% less energy used in this room.
**Step 4:** This is why storerooms are usually the BEST place to install a motion sensor - they are empty most of the time.

Smart lighting can be very effective in some spaces and almost useless in others. The key is matching the technology to how the room is actually used. In this worksheet you will calculate the energy savings of smart lighting in three different spaces.
What you should already know
*You should already know what motion sensors and daylight sensors do (see Worksheet 4A), and be confident calculating annual kWh and cost with Energy = Power × time.*

Smart lighting saves energy by reducing 'lights on' hours when the room is empty (motion sensors) or when there is enough daylight (daylight dimming). The QUANTITATIVE saving depends entirely on how the room is used.

MOTION SENSORS work best in spaces with LOW occupancy ratio. The occupancy ratio is the share of 'lights on' hours that are actually needed. A storage room with 4 hours of lighting but only 0.5 hours of occupancy has a ratio of 12.5% - meaning 87.5% potential saving. A classroom with 8 hours of lighting and 6 hours of occupancy has a ratio of 75% - only 25% potential saving.

TIME-OUT DELAY: motion sensors don't immediately switch off when the last movement stops. There is a delay (typically 3-15 minutes) so that the light doesn't flicker off if you sit still. This means real motion-sensor savings are slightly less than the theoretical maximum. A common rule of thumb: real 'lights on' time ≈ 1.2 × occupied time.

DAYLIGHT DIMMING: a light fixture with a daylight sensor doesn't necessarily switch off completely - it dims to maintain a target lux level. On average over a school year, a daylight-dimmed fixture in a classroom uses around 30% less energy than the same fixture without dimming, depending on window size and orientation.
PAYBACK: a motion sensor costs €30-€60 installed. A daylight dimmer costs €100-€150 installed. Whether either pays back depends on the room's annual lighting energy use.
*A school toilet has 6 LED tubes of 18 W. Lights are currently on 10 h/day for 190 school days. Toilet is occupied ~2 h/day. A €40 motion sensor is installed.*
**Step 1:** Current annual kWh: (6 × 18 / 1000) × 10 × 190 = 205.2 kWh
**Step 2:** With sensor: lights on ≈ 1.2 × 2 = 2.4 h/day. Annual kWh = (6 × 18 / 1000) × 2.4 × 190 = 49.2 kWh
**Step 3:** Saving: 205.2 − 49.2 = 156 kWh/year
**Step 4:** At €0.25/kWh: €39 saved per year
**Step 5:** Simple payback: 40 / 39 ≈ 1.0 years. Investment is highly attractive.
Occupancy ratio
Share of 'lights on' hours that are actually needed (occupied).

Modern school buildings increasingly use centrally-managed smart lighting: every fixture is addressable, sensors are networked, and lighting integrates with the school's HVAC and timetable systems. This worksheet asks you to design - on paper - a smart lighting strategy for one floor of your school. You will also confront the harder questions: is it worth the complexity? What about privacy and data?

*This worksheet assumes you have completed Worksheets 4A and 4B (or are confident with sensor types, occupancy reasoning and basic payback calculations). For the optional WP3 extension, basic familiarity with microcontrollers (Arduino, ESP32) is helpful.*

Modern smart-lighting systems are NETWORKED. Every fixture is individually addressable, sensors share data with multiple devices, and the system integrates with other building systems (HVAC, scheduling, security). This unlocks much larger savings than stand-alone sensors but introduces new design and ethical questions.

ZONING is the design step where you divide a building into 'lighting zones' - areas that should switch together. Zones are usually drawn around how spaces are USED, not where the wiring already runs. A good zoning plan considers occupancy patterns, daylight availability, control logic and emergency lighting requirements.

INTEGRATION with the school timetable, HVAC and security systems multiplies the value of the sensor data. A presence sensor used by lighting AND ventilation reduces hardware cost. Linking lighting control to the timetable means classrooms default to OFF when no class is scheduled, capturing waste that simple motion sensors miss (e.g. an empty room with someone walking through). The risk: a single faulty sensor or scheduling error can cascade across systems.

DATA AND PRIVACY: every networked sensor generates data. A motion sensor that knows when each room is occupied, combined with the timetable, can identify which students were in which room at which time. Under the GDPR (and increasingly under the EU AI Act for behaviour-monitoring systems), this is potentially personal data with all the obligations that follow: lawful basis, minimisation, retention limits, transparency. Energy savings do not exempt a school from data protection law.

DEPLOYMENT MATURITY: not all rooms benefit equally. The ROI of smart lighting drops sharply when occupancy ratio is high (regular classrooms used 6+ hours per day). Smart-lighting investment should target the rooms with the highest waste first.
*Design a zoning sketch for a single classroom with windows on the south side.*

**Step 1:** Zone 1: row of fixtures NEAREST the windows. Sensor: daylight (with manual override). Logic: dim to maintain 300 lux at desk level. On sunny days these fixtures may be at 20% power; on dark winter mornings 100%.
**Step 2:** Zone 2: row of fixtures FURTHEST from the windows. Sensor: motion + timetable. Logic: ON during scheduled lessons; motion-controlled outside scheduled hours; OFF otherwise.
**Step 3:** Zone 3: front-of-room fixture above the whiteboard. Sensor: separate switch (teacher control). Logic: always available, never automatic.
**Step 4:** Estimated saving vs. all-on baseline: 35-45% depending on weather and room use.
Zoning the floor
Get (or sketch) a plan of one floor of your school. Divide it into 'lighting zones' - areas that should switch together.

List your zones. For each, describe: typical use pattern, recommended sensor type (motion, daylight, both, none), recommended control logic (e.g. 'always on during school hours; off otherwise', 'motion sensor with 5-min timeout', 'daylight dimming + motion override').
Estimate the annual energy use of each zone before and after implementing your strategy. Use realistic LED wattages and your actual school day length.
Integration with other systems
Smart lighting can communicate with other building systems.

Describe one integration with the school's TIMETABLE system. (Example: 'Empty classrooms at 14:30 still have lights, even though no class is scheduled. Integration with the timetable means lights default to off in unscheduled rooms.') Estimate the additional saving.
Describe one integration with the school's HVAC system. (Example: presence detection used by both lighting and ventilation, reducing duplicated sensor cost.)
What is the risk of these integrations? (Example: a single faulty sensor switching off both lights AND ventilation in a classroom full of students.)
Privacy, data and ethics

A networked sensor that detects motion is also generating data: it knows when each room is occupied and for how long. Under the EU AI Act and the GDPR, this can become personal data if it can be linked to individuals.
Identify three pieces of information that motion-sensor data could leak about students or staff if combined with timetables.
Propose three concrete safeguards (technical or organisational) to limit privacy risk while still allowing energy savings.
Critically reflect: is the energy saving worth the privacy trade-off? When is it, and when is it not?
